Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein MD

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

NOTHING EVER REMAINS THE SAME because everything is suspended in time. Our world is ever changing, as well as our perceptions, our insights, and our understandings. The papers in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry attest to this truth. In this issue Bachrach tells us that the bedrock of psychoanalysis is its methodology. He refers to Rapaport's statement that what makes the analyst–analysand relationship specifically psychoanalytic is that it aims to carry communication to its “last consequences”—where the person who handles the relationship takes responsibility for eliminating “any and all” obstacles to communication no matter where they may lead.

Although Rapaport's description is as valid today as it was a half a century ago, our understanding of a psychoanalytic relationship is dramatically different. We have moved from an emphasis on an objective analyst, whose role it is to examine the patient's associations while more or less frustrating the patient's infantile desires, to an analyst who is immersed in the analytic field utilizing all his or her responses in promoting the progress of the analysis and the growth of the patient. The analyst is not isolated from his or her environment, culture, or gender but within the analytic situation brings these components into the elimination of “any and all” obstacles to communication no matter where they may lead.

Therefore it is impossible for the analyst in the clinical situation to be devoid of the influence of the exigencies of the external world. Reading the papers as a whole, we are shown the historical progression in psychoanalytic thinking and how this has influenced the availability of psychoanalytic patients. We see the psychoanalyst's approach to psychoanalysis; his or her optimism, ideals, and hopes are integral to the technique of the beginning of psychoanalysis. We are reminded that the analytic attitude must be directed toward helping patients with their agendas, not the psychoanalyst's. In sum we find the answer to “Where have all the psychoanalytic patients gone?” in the title of Wallerstein's paper. They haven't gone anywhere. Their presence is in the eyes of the beholders.

It's the Tortoise Race:

Long-Term Psychodynamic Psychotherapy with a High-Functioning Autistic Adolescent

Richard Bromfield PHD

Richard Bromfield

107 School Street
South Hamilton, MA 01982

Richard Bromfield  

THE INCREASINGLY COMMON KNOWLEDGE that autism is a developmental disorder of neurologic origin has led to an abandoning of psychodynamic treatments in favor of behavioral methods that train and educate the child. Most autistic children, lacking the language and symbolic capacities requisite for traditional psychotherapies, have benefited from this enlightenment. This change for the better, however, may not apply equally to more mildly autistic boys and girls.

First described as “autistically psychopathic” (Gilberg, 1985, pp. 389-390), some autistic children function at higher levels. Though showing the classic symptoms of more severe autism (e.g., exquisite anxiety, social awkwardness, peculiar speech patterns, odd nonverbal gesturing, communication deficits, ritualistic preoccupations, intolerance for change, and eccentric interests), they are considerably more socially involved and intellectually adept. Oft times having been classified as schizophrenic, atypical, and pervasively developmentally delayed, such children are now seen as representing the upper end of the autistic continuum (Bosch, 1962; Schopler, 1985; Szatmari, 1989)

Dr. Bromfield is a supervising psychologist at Harvard Medical School and the Massachusetts Mental Health Center.

Where Have All the Psychoanalytic Patients Gone? They're Still Here

Robert Wallerstein MD

Robert Wallerstein

290 Beach Rd.
Belvedere, CA 94920

Robert Wallerstein  

Abstract

I develop my argument concerning the question of where have all the patients gone in a sequence of three parts. First, I indicate, very briefly, the nature of the issue and the array of confluent socioeconomic causes—as they are usually outlined—that are held responsible for it. Then I take up the remedy for this problem posed by Arnold Rothstein in his book (1998), which is the trigger to this series of invited commentaries, and I indicate how I both appreciate the merits of his proposal to recast the issue as much as possible within a psychological framework, amenable to psychoanalytic influence, and nonetheless feel his approach to be based on a one-sided, and to that extent, a limited and flawed assessment of the problem, and therefore an only partially useful remedial perspective. And lastly, I offer an alternative view of the internal historical developments in psychoanalysis that have played their complementary role in the evolution of this perceived “crisis” and the alteration of perspectives, based on my account of our contenting current viewpoints on the nature of the relationship between psychoanalysis and its derivative psychoanalytic psychotherapies, that can perhaps promise a more effective counter to the crisis, despite the multiple external socioeconomic

Dr. Wallerstein is Professor Emeritus and Former Chairman, Department of Psychiatry, University of California San Francisco School of Medicine; Training and Supervising Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute

developments that are usually accorded causative primacy and that no doubt are indeed formidable.

Epilogue

Ellen Ruderman PHD PSYD , Estelle Shane PHD and Morton Shane MD

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

TO RETAIN ITS VITALITY AND DYNAMISM, psychoanalysis as a profession must continue to grow and change. New ideas and novel considerations for inclusion of innovative techniques in the armentarium of psychoanalytic treatment are all a part of this developmental process. An unexamined acceptance of and blind conformity to past ideas may lead to inflexibility, which often results in impasses in the treatment situation.

We as editors recognize that the subject of touch in analytic treatment is viewed not only as a sensitive and controversial topic, but indeed, has long been considered forbidden. As a result, it has remained an “untouched” area in the history of psychoanalysis. It gives us great pleasure, therefore, to be a part of bringing together for discussion and debate the differing views of twelve psychoanalysts who approach this delicate question in new and, one hopes, refreshing ways.

Once again, we are beholden to Patrick Casement in this endeavor. We appreciate his courage and forthrightness in bringing the topic to the attention of the psychoanalytic community's. We commend him as well for bringing forth with unflinching honesty his inner process with Mrs. B, whose treatment provided the genesis of this issue. His journey through the complications, pitfalls, and intense emotions associated with their work together, and the description of his careful and sensitive responsiveness to her, provided inspiration for all of our contributors. We thank him for his generosity of spirit in sharing so much of himself with his colleagues, and for the most able way he has responded to the contributions of his colleagues in his excellent retrospective.

Likewise, we are exceptionally grateful to our psychoanalyst contributors, not only for their careful consideration of the issues surrounding “touch,” and for their able treatment of this subject, but also for their willingness to share openly their thinking.

Clinical Protocol

Karen Bartholomew M.S.W. LCSW-C

Karen Bartholomew

500 West Montgomery Avenue
Rockville, MD 20850

Karen Bartholomew  

THE PATIENT, S,1 HAD BEEN with the Adolescent Inpatient Division for 10 months when the therapist she had been seeing took a 3-month maternity leave. The family of the patient was requesting intensive, four times a week psychotherapy with a therapist experienced in working with dissociative identity disorder.

S and I met on her hospital unit to see if we could work together. S had consulted with an expert on dissociative disorders the month prior to this meeting and understood she had a dissociative disorder and seven alter personalities. She was eager, she said, to get her emotions under control. She would get upset and “trash” her room for no apparent reason. She never wanted to see her parents again but was devastated if she couldn't talk to them on the phone or see them daily. We agreed to work together in her therapist's absence.

S had come to our facility at age 17 from a short-term hospital following a crisis in her foster care home. The foster care placement had been court ordered after S reported to a school counselor that her father had sexually abused her. The accusation, documented in the public record, was found unsubstantiated, but the Juvenile Court Judge was concerned and ordered the Department of Social Services to remain S's guardian until S's twenty-first birthday. S's parents were devastated but remained supportive of their daughter and her treatment.

Karen Bartholomew is the Director of Adult Services at CPC Health/Chestnut Lodge Hospital in Rockville, MD, and a doctoral candidate at Smith College School for Social Work in Northampton, MA.

Uncertainty in Treatment

THE CLINICAL TASK AT HAND is to provide what design clues we can for the building of a holding environment for a treatment that is trying. The transcripts present us a picture in words of an interpersonal situation rife with mistrust, confusion, dread, instability, fragmentation, vagueness, menace, difficulty and doubt. It is in fact very hard to tell just what is going on. The transcripts succeed admirably at recruiting the reader into this atmosphere, so that the reader too feels frustrated and confused.

In fact, as I read these transcripts, my mind wandered to works by Samuel Beckett, where nothing much happens; whatever happens is tedious and trivial and irritating, yet it keeps going on, continuing itself with incredible tenacity. Beckett, of course, was inspired by both vaudeville and reality. These transcripts rob us of any sense of conviction as to there being solid ground under our feet. The brief history presented is a tragic and daunting one, leading us to reflect on matters of history, vanity, and perhaps even on the intrinsic perversity of our own species. The history involves neglect, severe limitations in early investment and physical and psychological care, social and cultural dislocation of a massive kind, trauma, and so forth.

Dr. Lewin is in private practice in Towson, MD, and teaches and supervises residents at Sheppard Pratt.

Melvin Bornstein MD Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Old ideas give way slowly for they are more than abstract logical forms and categories, they are habits, predispositions, and deeply ingrained attitudes of aversion and preference. Moreover the conviction persists, though history shows it to be a hallucination, that all questions that the human mind has asked are questions that can be answered in terms of the alternatives that the questions themselves present.

But in fact intellectual progress usually occurs through shear abandonment of the questions and the alternatives that they assume, abandonment that results from their decreasing vitality and change of urgent interest. We do not solve them we get over them.—John Dewey.

Response to Commentaries

Karen Bartholomew MSW LCSW-C

Karen Bartholomew

Karen Bartholomew  

I WOULD LIKE TO EXPRESS MY APPRECIATION for the thoughtful comments of Kluft, Lewin, and Saakvitne in reviewing my clinical protocol of three consecutive sessions with a very complex and challenging young woman. Each response deserves its own response, but in the interest of space I would like to note some connecting themes among the three responders and give clinical examples of the therapy with S to support these themes.

Lewin and Saakvitne comment on attachment as central to the work with S. To this day, S reenacts her early disrupted attachment and traumatic attachment in her relationship with me. There have been many times when I have struggled to find the optimism Saakvitne expressed in her final paragraph regarding my relationship with S. More often, I am seen as the complex other, a threat and a promise as Lewin stated. During one of my separations from S, which occurred during her hospitalization at another facility, S recounted to her therapist at that hospital a fantasy of mutual acting out as if it had happened. The therapist understood this was fantasy, and I was able to confront S with her wish to have me be closer to her and also her wish to destroy me. The scenario was consistent with the possibility that S may have wished to destroy me in order to somehow possess me forever, as Dr. Lewin posited.

Saakvitne writes of S's fear of being left, her need to leave, and her need to control those who might leave her as central in understanding her actions and impulsivity. In fact, a series of impulsive actions on S's part resulted in a lengthy stay at a state hospital.

Epilogue

Using the DES-II

Richard Chefetz MD

Richard Chefetz

Richard Chefetz  

THIS EXPLANATION IS PROVIDED so that you may become familiar with the Dissociative Experiences Scale (DES), version II. A series of references are listed so that you may have a resource for looking at some of the work done with the Dissociative Experiences Scale (Bernstein, 1986; Ross, 1990; Carlson, 1993a, b). Effort was made to include references readily available to most readers. The DES is a screening tool in the evaluation of persons thought to have post-traumatic or dissociative symptomatology. It is not a diagnostic tool. The DES, and a short manual on its use, is available from the Sidran Foundation at 410.825.8888 (email: sidran@access.digex.net) or on the Internet at http://www.sidran.org.

The DES can be used to screen for dissociative experience in large populations in a short period of time, or as an introduction to differential clinical formulation for the clinician who is otherwise unfamiliar with dissociative phenomena. The more experienced clinician may find it a time saver. Its most useful application may actually be in the post-test discussion of the patient's responses to different items on the scale. In my clinical practice, I find that discussion of the rationale of answers to questions on the DES quickly opens an inquiry into the private experience of the person with dissociative adaptations. In combination with questions from the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Dissociative Disorders (Steinberg, 1993), the thoughtful clinician may find a comprehensive compendium of language to use in defining a mental status examination which includes posttraumatic symptoms related to dissociation.

To obtain a raw score for the DES, total the numerical sum of responses for all 28 items on the DES. In order to obtain a proper score, all 28 items must be endorsed. While some persons may have questions about the meaning of an item, you may not explain the meaning to the patient. Instruct patients to do the best job they can in understanding the item and to endorse it in the manner in which they interpret it. You may advise them to mark that item for discussion in the post-test period. Divide the raw score by 28. This is the test score.

Prologue

Eloise Agger DSW

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

IT IS ENTIRELY FITTING that this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, one of the first appearing in the 21st century, should deal with hatred and its significance in human development. The 20th century saw two world wars and many minor wars, no less venal for their nationalistic aims and political rationales, which have bruised, wounded and/or exterminated countless individuals and devalued groups. Even though hapless victims of war and interpersonal violence suffer impoverishment of the personality and depletion of the spirit, the thirst for power, mastery, and revenge lives on in the minds and behavior of the winning aggressors and those who must take their only comfort in surrender.

As one of the emotions usually associated with aggression, hatred fascinates, alarms, and repels us. We hesitate to acknowledge it in ourselves, yet are surrounded by its aura in our daily lives. Who has escaped the pain inflicted by a child's hurled assault, “I hate you, Mom (Dad)!” And who has not felt the shame of feeling such a base impulse toward a colicky infant. What about the revulsion we experience at reading about the teenaged boy who murdered his accomplished sister, burned down the family home with his mother in it, and then blithely set off to return to college? President Clinton, in September 1998, remorsefully spoke of the effects of hatred, “The anger, the resentment, the bitterness, the desire for recrimination against people you believe have wronged you, they harden the heart and deaden the spirit, and lead to self-inflicted wounds.” And, those who loved to hate this last president of the century, would have claimed he spoke guilefully, without remorse.

The precursors of hatred arise from the infant's response to what William James (1890) called the “booming buzzing confusion” that assaults the infant's sensorium at perception's birth.

Epilogue

Susan Epstein CSW

Susan Epstein

Susan Epstein  

THE MYSTERY THAT IS AUTISM INSPIRES INQUIRY, attempts to understand and to explain. Its intractable nature can inspire desperation or the desire to conquer and defeat—or both. This combination of human responses to autism has led to an exceptional amount of hypothesizing about etiology and treatment. Some of that drive has led to the development of important advances and some to the pursuit of “fringe” theories and treatments supported only by anecdotal evidence and the desire to believe.

The historical efforts to explain and cure autism were not the psychoanalytic tradition's finest hour. The seductive pull to force a fit of phenomenology to theory is one that most of us have experienced at some time in our careers. It is, obviously, something that must be zealously guarded against in the name, not only of those we aim to help, but the field of psychoanalysis as well.

Does the assumption, on my part and those of the authors in this issue, that disorders of the autistic spectrum are neurobiological in origin justify a rejection of any application of psychodynamic thinking to the problem? Part of the answer lies in a question that cannot be adequately explored in this issue, although it was touched on by Greenspan in his article. Autism is not a singular entity. Individuals are affected not only in level of severity, but in a variety of presentations as well. Individual development both acts on and is acted upon by autism. Intervention must be geared to the complex matrix of each individual.

The clinical interventions described in this issue will, to this writer's mind, be effective only for those on the higher end of the autistic spectrum and should not be seen as evidence of their value all along the spectrum. Modified dynamic formulations for patients with sufficient expressive and receptive language, cognitive abilities, and capacity for relationship may lead to helpful intervention for some higher functioning individuals.

Should Analytic Patients Be “Created”? Reflections on Arnold Rothstein's Psychoanalytic Technique and the Creation of Analytic Patients

Susan Lazar MD

Susan Lazar

9105 Quintana Drive
Bethesda, MD 20817

Susan Lazar  

The five points of Arnold Rothstein's interesting monograph are each discussed and critiqued in this article. In particular, Rothstein is commended for his commitment to expanding the availability of an intensive, psychoanalytic treatment for a broad spectrum of patients who may often be very difficult to engage. Rothstein also accounts for difficulties in engaging analytic patients from obstacles in the attitudes of analysts such as a latent lack of conviction about the efficacy of psychoanalysis and from overly restricted stereotypes about the spectrum of appropriate patients. He recommends a flexibility of technique and accommodation to the needs of patients with which this author agrees.

Others of Rothstein's observations and recommendations seem more problematic. Specifically, issue is taken with his suggestion that analysts attempt to provide a trial of psychoanalysis for all nonpsychotic patients and to begin on a

Dr. Lazar is Supervising and Training Analyst, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences, Georgetown University School of Medicine, and George Washington University School of Medicine.

556

less intensive basis only within the frame of interpreting prospective patients' objections as a resistance. This author also disagrees with Rothstein's interpretation that patients resist the offer of a psychoanalysis out of a self-defeating masochistic enactment that needs interpretation. Case examples are provided that belie this overly generalized interpretation. Additionally, this author critiques the metapsychological assumptions underlying this particular mode of interpreting a reluctance to begin psychoanalysis.

While commending Rothstein's therapeutic goals and recommended flexibility of technique, this author would also stress a fundamental concern about the patient's conscious and unconscious experience of the analyst's agenda. In other words, rather than working toward the analyst's goal of establishing a psychoanalytic situation, emphasis is placed instead on the basic right of patients to proceed in a manner that respects their sovereignty over how intensively they may choose to work. Therefore, in contradistinction to Rothstein's suggestions, it is recommended that the analyst's primary focus should be to provide an availability to work on the patient's conflicts and developmental needs with a respect for the timing of their emergence and expression within a treatment frame that invites but does not prematurely elicit and confront. By proceeding in this way a patient's salient dynamics will be allowed to emerge “organically” instead of being hastened prematurely in reaction to the analyst's insistence on the rightness of a particular schedule or manner of proceeding. This author believes that with this approach more, rather than fewer, patients will be able to accept the recommendation of an intensive psychoanalytic treatment.

Trauma impels people both to withdraw from close relationships and to seek them desperately. The profound disruption in basic trust, the common feelings of shame, guilt, and inferiority, and the need to avoid reminders of the trauma that might be found in social life, all foster withdrawal from close relationships. The traumatized person therefore frequently alternates between isolation and anxious clinging to others [Herman, 1992, p. 56].

LONG-TERM GROUP PSYCHOTHERAPY is an important and potentially healing component of a multimodal therapeutic approach for women who are survivors of childhood abuse. The conceptual framework presented is derived from portions of different models of group therapy and abuse dynamics. Interactions of the members of the group and the interventions of the co-therapists are illustrated. The clinical dilemmas encountered by the therapists are depicted. Significant issues of group process and recovery are addressed.

Individuals who suffer the long-term effects of childhood abuse present a major public health problem. Numerous studies indicate that two-thirds of the female patients receiving psychiatric care reported a history of early physical, emotional, and/or sexual abuse (Chu, 1990). Judith Lewis Herman (1992) in her book Trauma and Recovery stated, “Because these traumas affect every aspect of human functioning, treatment must be comprehensive. There is no single efficacious ‘magic bullet’ for the traumatic syndromes” (p. 156). It is vital, therefore, to provide a survivor of childhood abuse a variety of therapeutic approaches if mental health clinicians are to deliver effective treatment.

Judith DiNunno, MSW, LCSW-C is the senior therapist at Threshold Services, Inc., Silver Spring, MD, and adjunct clinician at Chestnut Lodge Hospital, Rockville, MD.

Epilogue

Eloise Agger DSW

Eloise Agger

Eloise Agger  

READING THE ARTICLES IN THIS ISSUE, we are privileged to experience new ways of thinking about the many shapes of hate and hatred that plague the therapeutic process. The authors represented here have sanitized the intense affects surrounding hate, via various clinical, behavioral, and literary explorations into the early root systems found in instinctual, neuorobiological, intrapsychic, and interpersonal life, as did Kohut and his followers for narcissism and its emotional satellites. By focussing on the rewards and adaptive benefits of hatred, we see, regardless of the author's particular theoretical orientation, how affective bonds fueled by hatred may prove stronger and more resistant to therapeutic dilution that those attachments based on affectionate strivings.

Have we found an answer to why, as analysts, our hateful feelings appear more problematic than say our sexual, competitive, envious, maternal, guilty, or even dependent countertransference responses Winnicott refers to the detable proposition of “objective and justified hatred” and wonders how the analyst should manage this emotion, whether to bear it silently or find a way to communicate it to the patient. Again, why is our hatred any different from other seemingly negative or unfriendly feelings?

We are surprised when our patients assault us with claims about our unheimlich procedures and surroundings, the very same conditions that we so conscientiously invested with heimlich intent, assuming with minimal self-deception, that our goal was to create a safe, holding environment. In his paper on the “incanny,” Freud (1919) discusses this German term, heimlich, loosely translated as homely, familiar, native, as well as its opposite, unheimlich, which can be experienced as strange, foreign, uneasy, even sinister, or uncanny.

A Case Illustration

Joseph Lichtenberg MD

Joseph Lichtenberg

1616 18th Street, NW

Joseph Lichtenberg  

SISTER MARY, A 42-YEAR-OLD large, heavyset school teacher and nun began her first hour of analysis by exclaiming as soon as she settled on the couch that it was the ugliest, flimsiest, most uncomfortable piece of furniture she had ever seen. I must be some fucking idiot to select such a piece of trash. That went for the rest of my office. It was cold and unwelcoming. I was supposed to be so good with my books and papers, but what fucking good is a lot of shitty knowledge if you can't be a human being?

This invective, stated in an angry, spite-filled tone, poured out of her in a continuous flow throughout the first hour. I was dumbfounded! Nothing in the several consultative hours prepared me for it. I did remember that, on the phone when she called for an appointment, she had said she had been told by the referring psychiatrist that I was someone who could handle her. As she went on, I felt a mixture of annoyance and amusement: annoyed at her attack on my couch, a custom-designed Danish import I was proud of; amused at the inventiveness of her foul-mouthed assault. I knew of nothing to say and wondered what to expect at the end of the hour, but she left without incident.

The next day, she entered, her nose in the air, and began where she had left off. I was more prepared but equally puzzled.

Some Considerations of “Hate” and a Reconsideration of the Death Instinct

James Grotstein MD

James Grotstein

James Grotstein  

HATE IS A MORE SEVERE MANIFESTATION OF ANGER. Whereas anger seems usually to be transient, hate is more perseverating and implies a personal (narcissistic) injury to its bearer. It would seem that hate stands to anger as melancholia stands to mourning. There is no issue of self-esteem in mourning or in anger, but there is in melancholia (Freud, 1917) and hate. It is interesting to learn the phantasies that accompany hate.

It is my impression that the infant phenomenologically begins his career of negativity with angry protests. His first experience, as a matter of fact, that of birth, he meets with a cry of discomfort, presumably for losing his wonderful symmetrical erstwhile home. His anger is his protest—what is felt by him to be, at the moment, intolerable. His demonstrations of anger, consequently, are protests to his “quartermaster”1-mother to correct a situation that is felt to be intolerable at that moment. In other words, anger to the infant is a signal of distress to himself and to his partner, the latter of whom is less helpless than he and therefore better able to correct the situation.

Dr. Grotstein is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, UCLA School of Medicine.

1“Quartermaster” is an ancient naval term for the one aboard ship who is in charge of room assignments and maintenance. I am using this term here as a subset of the mother's function as a holding environment or mirroring selfobject. The infant's cry can be translated as, “Damn it! Find me better quarters than these—ones like where I used to be when I got perfect womb service!”462

George Allison  

This paper explores a number of reasons for the shortage of patients available for psychoanalysis in recent years. A particular focus is on the possible connection of “hard times” for psychoanalytic practice with the flowering theoretical diversity in our field over the past 30 years in the United States. While there is undoubted enrichment from this theoretical ferment, the author questions the benefit of its influence on technique and outcome in full-scale psychoanalysis. The distinctions between psychoanalysis and psychotherapy are increasingly blurred. The argument is made that theoretical diversity as a concurrent phenomenon with the shortage of patients for full psychoanalysis fits in with the homogenization of psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy as a practical response to the crisis. A section of the paper also deals with the author's view of the impact of patient shortage and theoretical diversity on the policies and standards of psychoanalytic training institutes in the United States. Theoretical diversity and multidisciplinary inclusionism are consistent with contemporary culture but may also lead to a homogenization and egalitarianism in both psychoanalytic treatment and training, which

Dr. Allison is Training and Supervising Analyst, Seattle Institute for Psychoanalysis; Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of Washington.

Prologue

Ellen Ruderman PHD Psy.D. , Estelle Shane PHD and Morton Shane MD

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

WE ARE PLEASED TO PRESENT to Psychoanalytic Inquiry readers this issue on Touch in the Psychoanalytic Situation. Using as a focal point for discussion Patrick Casement's seminal paper, “Some Pressures on the Analyst for Physical Contact During the Reliving of an Early Trauma,” published in 1982, our contributors have considered explored this controversial question from many divergent contemporary perspectives.

We would contend that all mental health practitioners have been required to struggle with this concern at one time or another during their careers, making these contributions clinically valuable.

We want to take this opportunity to express our gratitude to all of our contributors, but especially to Patrick Casement who first pioneered an open exploration of this question and who continues to lead the way in his retrospective commentary on his own work and the other papers contained in this issue.

Stanley Greenspan

7201 Glenbrook Road

Stanley Greenspan  

OVER THE PAST 20 YEARS we have formulated a model of early ego development that integrates biological differences, developmental stages, interaction patterns and wishes and affects. Our approach to assessing and intervening with children with autistic spectrum disorders is based on this model, which emerged from work with infants, young children, and their families. Understanding early ego development served as a foundation for a therapeutic program that has enabled a subgroup of children with autistic spectrum diagnoses to become engaging, communicative, verbal, creative, and empathetic (Greenspan and Wieder, 1977, 1998; Greenspan, 1992a). Applying developmental concepts in clinical work has also suggested a core psychological deficit in autistic spectrum disorder and the components of a comprehensive approach to intervention.

Basic Concepts

Before we describe our work with children with autistic spectrum diagnoses, it is necessary to provide a brief discussion of the basic concepts that inform this work.

Dr. Greenspan is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Pediatrics, and Behavioral Sciences at George Washington University Medical School and Chairman of the Interdisciplinary Council for Developmental and Learning Disorders.

The Meanings of Touch in Psychoanalysis

A Time for Reassessment

James Fosshage PHD

James Fosshage

330 West 58th Street, Suite 200
New York, NY 10019

James Fosshage  

PSYCHOANALYSIS TRADITIONALLY HAS PLACED an almost total interdiction on physical touch between patient and analyst within the analytic arena. Yet touch, based on our largest sensory organ, the skin, provides a fundamental and elaborate form of communication. So important is tactile stimulation for development and maintenance of physiological and physiological and psychological regulations of persons of all ages are “righted” through physical holding and touch.

Physical touch within psychoanalysis has been hotly debated beginning with Freud and Ferenczi. Ferenczi (1953) felt that nurturing touch could facilitate the analysis by helping a patient to tolerate pain that was characterologically defended against. Freud flet that physical contact would almost certainly lead to sexual enactments. In the heat of this controversy, Ferenczi's patient (Clara Thompson) boasted to one of Freud's patients that she was allowed to kiss “Papa Ferenczi” anytime she wished. Freud strongly objected, admonishing Ferenczi that this sort of behavior would inevitably lead to a downward spiral to full sexual engagement.

Dr. Fosshage is Board Director and Faculty, National Institute for the Psychotherapies, NYC; Founding Faculty Member, Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity, NYC: and Clinical Professor of Psychology, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis.

Coconstructing Mother—Infant Distress

The Microsynchrony of Maternal Impingement and Infant Avoidance in the Face-to-Face Encounter

Beatrice Beebe PHD

Beatrice Beebe

Beatrice Beebe  

IN THE FIRST YEAR OF LIFE, the infant shows a remarkable range of aversion, withdrawal, and avoidance, but not hatred. Using Lichtenberg's (this volume) definitions of hatred, such as detest, abhor, ill will, vengeance, and retaliation, we will see that it is not possible for the infant to have these emotions until there is a symbolic mind. Therefore, in the infant I will be addressing aversion and avoidance, but not hatred, based on analyses of face-to-face play at approximately three to four months of life. In one sense, infant aversion and withdrawal are completely usual and adaptive coping capacities. From time to time all infants look away and turn away in order to regulate arousal back down to a comfortable range. On the other hand, more extreme forms of infant aversion and withdrawal can be observed, particularly in relation to maternal overstimulation and intrusion. The mother of course is capable of hatred, but in the range of disturbances I see, most mothers want to love their babies. Maternal hatred is extremely rare. What is not rare, however, and is of utmost importance to the origins of early psychopathology, is maternal intrusion and impingement.

Dr. Beebe is Associate Clinical Professor of Psychology, New York State Psychiatric Institute; faculty, Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity, New York City.

The delights of gratified hatred are among the fiercest and most ardent that the heart can feel.

Balzac, Cousin Bette

FOR A CONTEMPORARY PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY of hatred to emerge, we must clarify the distinction between hatred and aggressive drive and between hatred and narcissistic rage. Stated differently, we must reconsider whether hatred is largely a derivative of aggressive drive or a discharge product of it as ego psychology often implies. Or is hatred best conceptualized through the viewpoint of object relationalists as a result of projective identification? Or is hatred a fragmentation product resulting from empathic failures that threaten self-cohesion leading to narcissistic rage as self psychologists have maintained? Basing the attempt to reconceptualize hatred on a motivational systems theory, we look to the “rewards” of hatred to identify the powerful ubiquitous place hating takes in human existence and to distinguish “hating” in common usage from “hatred.

Karen Saakvitne  

ASI READ BARTHOLOMEW'S COMPELLING PRESENTATION of her relationship and work with her patient, S, two thoughts recur. First, I am grateful that possibilities for long-term intensive care remain in a “healthcare” climate that has all but eradicated such opportunities. I see S as a client who can especially benefit from such a setting for reasons that overlap with and also differ from those presented. The careful, thoughtful work occurring over time that has been her treatment is clearly invaluable.

Second, I note how our psychoanalytic theories have become less developmental in focus. In particular I struggle with the strange absence of attachment theory in formulations of clients with severe early trauma and loss. Bartholomew's protocol offers persuasive evidence for dissociative identity disorder (DID) (and possibly Dissociative Disorder, Not Otherwise Specified [DDNOS]) as an attachment disorder. The central theme is abandonment, but the central dynamic is attachment. In my comments, I will primarily be applying such a framework to my understanding of S and her relationship with Karen B.

Before I go further, I'd like to remind the reader of the limitations of our format.

Dr. Saakvitne is Clinical Director, Traumatic Stress Institute/Center for Adult and Adolescent Psychotherapy, South Windsor, CT and coauthor of a number of books and articles on the treatment of trauma.

Developing a Psychoanalytic Practice

Stephen Bernstein MD

Stephen Bernstein

146 Wallis Road
Chestnut Hill, MA 02467
Bethesda, MD 20817

Stephen Bernstein  

This paper examines two method of developing a psychoanalytic practice. The first is an “internal” approach that helps a patient make the transition from therapy to analysis with the same analyst. This may be accomplished by attenuating the patient's unconscious fears of analysis as a facilitator of an anticipated regressive loss of control and as a reactivator of feared desires and impulses. Increased motivation for analysis may also result from a therapy that leads the patient to an awareness that an ongoing level of distress is internal, together with the experience of a deepened therapy and of the analyst as safe and potentially providing relief. The second method of developing an analytic practice is an “external” approach that provides others, such as analytic, mental health, medical, and academic colleagues, an experience of the analyst as person and some idea of the type of work he or she does.

That Is the Question

Alex Holder PHD

Alex Holder

Körnerstrasse 17
22301 Hamburg, Germany

Alex Holder  

PATRICK CASEMENT'S “Some Pressures on the Analyst for Physical Contact During the Reliving of an Early Trauma” (1982) presents a welcome opportunity to comment on several aspects of it within the overall topic of this special issue on touch. I intend to do this in the first part of this paper. The second part will be devoted to a critical evaluation of psychoanalytical body psychotherapy as propagated by some of its exponents. The last part offers some thoughts on the differences in regard to the subject and meaning of touch in the analytical work with children as compared with adults.

I

The link between the subject of touch and the classical rule of abstinence is an obvious one, and Casement indeed opens his paper with a reference to it, suggesting that exceptions might be considered in the case of deeply regressed patients. In the case of the patient he presents in his paper, one might argue that it was precisely his refusal—or rather the withdrawal of his offer—for her to hold his hand, if necessary, that plunged her into a deep regression that, at one point, reached psychotic proportions.

Dr. Holder is a Member, Training and Supervising Analyst, German and British Psychoanalytical Societies; and coauthor of The Patient and the Analyst and Freud's Models of the Mind.

Discussion of Patrick Casement's Learning from the Patient

Barbara Pizer EDD ABPP

Barbara Pizer

152 Brattle Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

Barbara Pizer  

WHEN I WAS A YOUNG GIRL, my mother took me to the burn unit in a hospital. Her friend's two-year-old son, Ben, had reached up to the stove and pulled the kettle of boiling water all over himself, scalding more than half of his little body. I had known Ben as an affectionate, cuddly boy, and what stood out for me was the sight of him now, totally encased in a protective see-through bubble—pleading blue eyes, a tentative smile, an arm reaching toward me with fingers outstretched but unable to touch the side of his plastic airfilled container. Ben was aching for contact but was too burned to be touched. Today, in my consulting room, when I sit with people who have been severely scalded by intrusive or withholding caregivers, when I witness persons deprived of sufficient recognition and self-affirming contact, I often use my memory of Ben as metaphor. I might say something like, “I sense that your body is aching, and I sense the pain in your eyes, and I'm reminded of a burn victim reaching out for contact but knowing it's too painful to be touched.” I have also come upon a related metaphor that seems to resonate with another kind of person—a person who has adapted to untenable neglect with counterphobic independence and the appearance of narcissistic retreat.

Dr. Pizer is Faculty, Supervising Psychoanalyst, Massachusetts Institute for Psychoanalysis; Instructor, Harvard Medical School.

The Concept of Multiple Function and Dissociation

Paul Gedo PHD

Paul Gedo

Chestnut Lodge Hospital

Paul Gedo  

TO BE A CLINICIAN IN OUR TIMES is to be aware of the ubiquity of disavowal and its still more primitive variant, dissociation, in the psyches of our patients and, through them, in ourselves. At Chestnut Lodge, where we work intensively with severely troubled persons, we are occasionally afforded the opportunity to observe the developmental vicissitudes of dissociative phenomena across a long-term treatment. This essay reflects my experiences in therapy that I conducted with Ms. Q for 8 years, until she moved out of state. My aim is not to detail the case, but to reflect on our work, and particularly on Ms. Q's extensive use of disavowal and dissociation, through the prism of Waelder's (1930) concept of “multiple function.”

Ms. Q transferred to Chestnut Lodge from a hospital in her home state. She had been engaged in treatment for a decade, including one long-term and many brief hospitalizations. She suffered from a severe mood disorder characterized by occasional bursts of manic grandiosity and paranoid thinking, alternating with more typical states of depression, emptiness, and self-destructive preoccupations.

Dr. Gedo is Chief Psychologist and Director of Psychology Training, Chestnut Lodge Hospital/C.P.C. Health, and an Advanced Candidate, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute.

PSYCHOANALYSIS AND THE STUDY OF DISSOCIATION and the dissociative disorders have had a long, if uneasy, uncomfortable, and often mutually avoidant relationship (Berman, 1981; Kluft, 1995b). Ernest Jones (1953) reports that the index case of the “Studies on Hysteria” (Breuer and Freud, 1893-1895), Fraulein Anna O, suffered a condition with “the presence of two distinct states of consciousness: one a fairly normal one, the other that of a naughty and troublesome child, rather like Morton Prince's famous case of Sally Beauchamps” (p. 223). Breuer and Freud initially hypothesized that “the splitting of consciousness which is so striking in the well-known classical cases under the form of ‘double consciousness’ is present to a rudimentary degree in every hysteria, and that a tendency to such a dissociation, and with it the emergence of abnormal states of consciousness … is the basic phenomenon of this neurosis” (p. 12).

Hatred and Its Rewards

A Discussion

Glen Gabbard MD

Glen Gabbard

P. O. Box 829
Topeka, KS 66601-0829

Glen Gabbard  

IN THIS DISCUSSION I WILL COMMENT on two contributions in this volume: the theoretical paper by Shapard and Lichtenberg and the clinical presentation of Sister Mary by Lichtenberg. Shapard and Lichtenberg have questioned the traditional linkage between murderous hate and the aggressive drive. Their motivational systems view of development is one that eschews reductionism. The point of this model is that motivation, such as hating another person, is a complex phenomenon. A plethora of interacting forces contribute to the patient's behavior and experience. Their view is explicitly pluralistic in this regard and is in keeping with the fundamental psychoanalytic notion of multiple determination.

Freud himself had some serious doubts about the linkage of hate and the aggressive drive as well. In his 1915 paper “Instincts and Their Vicissitudes,” he noted, “The case of love and hate acquires a special interest from the circumstance that it refuses to be fitted into our scheme of the instincts” (p. 133). He noted that loving and hating were clearly not instinctual drives, but rather described attitudes that one person held toward another. Freud realized it was inappropriate to refer to an instinct as “hating” an object. To try to force his conceptualization into his theory, he concluded that it was the total ego that harbored feelings of hate toward objects. He postulated that the ego hated those objects that produced unpleasurable feelings.

The Problem and Place of Physical Contact in Analytic Work

Some Reflections on Handholding in the Analytic Situation

James McLaughlin MD

James McLaughlin

220 N. Bellefield Avenue
Apt. 403
Pittsburgh, PA 15213

James McLaughlin  

PHYSICAL CONTACT OF ANY SORT between patient and therapist in the analytic relationship continues to be an unsettled technical and theoretical dilemma for psychoanalysis. The problem has long been complicated by its implicit linkage to the liabilities of actual physical intimacy, sexual and aggressive, between the analytic pair.

In reminder: between 1911 and 1914 Freud provided a binding technical and theoretical rationale for the analyst to remain detached and unyielding in his objectivity, to stand fast against acting upon libidinal desires for gratification stirred in either party (Freud, 1912, pp. 112-114). Above all, both parties were to speak, not act.

This assumed authority of the analyst's superior knowledge was supported by a persuasive theory about what made analysis work. This theory posited, then accepted as a given, that the analyst's consistent frustration of the patient's libidinal impulses was the way to achieve the desired regression of the patient to those earlier psychic states in which crucial pathological formations had been set in place. Only from within this analyst-induced frustration state could the patient truly rework old pathology in the benign presence of the neutrally posed analyst.

Dr. McLaughlin is Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst, Pittsburgh Psychoanalytic Institute, and Former Director, Pittsburgh Psychoanalytic Institute.

A Contextual Consideration of Boundaries From a Developmental Systems Self Psychology Perspective

Morton Shane MD , Estelle Shane PHD and Mary Gales MD

Mary Gales

1800 Fairburn Avenue

Mary Gales  

THIS PAPER, LIKE THE OTHERS IN THIS ISSUE, is inspired by the boundary dilemma faced by Patrick Casement when he was asked to meet the request of his traumatized patient to have her hand held at a crucial time in their analytic work. This question of touch, of physical contact, and its place in the analytic situation is complex and is interconnected with larger issues pertaining to boundaries in general. One's response to this issue depends in no small part on the theoretical model the analyst plays. Our paper is written from a developmental systems self psychology perspective (Shane, Shane, and Gales, 1997) in which all questions of boundary, including that of touch, are conceptualized contextually, emerging from within a particular psychoanalytic dyad and shaped by it.

Working with the Person with Dissociative Identity Disorder

Richard Chefetz MD

Richard Chefetz

4612 49th Street NW
Washington, DC 20016-4321
chefetz@erols.com

Richard Chefetz  

IN THE TREATMENT OF A PERSON with dissociative identity disorder (DID), both patient and therapist are confronted with major challenges to their routine views of having a “self,” being an “I.” To become engaged in this work, the therapist might anticipate the potential alteration of the identity and meaning of nearly everything that could be perceived as part of being human. Little of what we take for granted about our routine experience of a day is untouched. The treatment of DID is an exploration of distortions in the experience of experiencing.

The diagnostic criteria for this disorder, whether drawn from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (American Psychiatric Association, 1994) or the Structured Clinical Interview for Dissociative Disorders (SCID-D) (Steinberg, 1993) shed little light on the paths that need to be illuminated for the therapeutic dyad to succeed in the work of healing. Many clinicians are wary of treating a person with this diagnosis.

The Issue of Touch

A Retrospective Overview

Patrick Casement MA

Patrick Casement

122 Mansfield Road
London NW3 2JB England

Patrick Casement  

I AM DELIGHTED THAT THE MATTER OF “TOUCH” is at last being properly debated in this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry and that my paper “Some Pressures on the Analyst for Physical Contact….” has been used as a take-off point for this discussion.

One thing that strikes me immediately is how interesting it is to find that an analyst in a paper, as with an analyst in a consulting room, can be used to represent positions that are allocated to him by those wishing to engage with particular positions. I am happy for this to be so, even though it means tolerating a fair degree of being misrepresented in the process, and I am therefore especially grateful for having this opportunity now to respond to that use of my paper.

Also, as with any analyzing that takes place in the absence of the patient (known as “wild analysis”), we can see how it can easily happen that assumptions begin to be made about an absent analyst/author, which, going unchecked, can lead to constructions that may end up rather wide of the mark. But, in this case, it does not matter, for two reasons: first, that I am fortunately in a position to respond (which is often not the case when debate takes place unknown to the person concerned) and, second, because this “use” of me as the analyst of Mrs. B may be providing important opportunities for debate with the positions represented.

Patrick J. Casement is Training and Supervising Analyst, British Psycho-Analytical Society; Author, On Learning, from the Patient (1985) and Further Learning from the Patient (1990), both published in Learning from the Patient (1990).

Meeting the Needs of Young Autistic Children and Their Families in a Multidisciplinary Therapeutic Nursery Model

Doris Allen EdD and Lois Mendelson PHD

Lois Mendelson

411 E. Clinton Avenue
Tenafly, NJ 07670

Lois Mendelson  

AUTISM, A SERIOUS DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER that presents in children before the age of three, has a history of diagnostic confusion, prognostic uncertainty, and a never-ending array of treatment options. It is not at all unusual for parents to receive conflicting diagnoses if they take their atypical preschool child to several different professionals. Autism, nonautistic pervasive developmental disorder (PDD or PDD-NOS), mental retardation, developmental language disorder, attention deficit with or without hyperactivity, emotional disturbance, or static encephalopathy may be diagnosed—all in the same child. No wonder the parents are perplexed, frightened, and, in most instances, devastated. After receiving a diagnosis of autism, parents are faced with the twin dilemmas of where to turn for a fuller understanding of this disorder and how to decide which kind of treatment would be best for their child. The choice of treatment is, of course, critical, and there are many options to choose from.

Dr. Allen is Associate Clinical Professor in Psychiatry, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, and Director, JCC on the Palisades Therapeutic Nursery.

Autism and the Psychoanalyst

Theodore Shapiro MD

Theodore Shapiro

Payne Whitney Clinic, Box 140
New York Presbyterian Hospital—Cornell Medical Center
525 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Theodore Shapiro  

It WAS NOT BY CHANCE that psychoanalysts were drawn to the problems of children who were diagnosed as autistic during the 1950s. It was a time when analysts were trying to solve the mysteries of everything from neuroses to schizophrenia by application of the psychoanalytic method—and this despite the fact that Freud considered his method to be most apt for neuroses. It was a time of experimentation with the clinical application of psychoanalysis, which was applied to any unyielding disorder of behavior or emotion with the hope of resolution or cure.

During the prior decade, as this general enthusiasm and therapeutic zeal was growing within psychoanalysis, there were nonanalytic physicians and pediatricians who were describing new syndromes and disorders that were considered to be inborn and not psychogenic. One such discovery was made by Leo Kanner (1943) at Johns Hopkins in 1943. He described Early Infantile Autism as a disorder that was characterized by an “inborn disturbance in affective contact” that consequently interfered with social interaction and language development and provided for only a narrow repertoire of play and other behaviors that appeared as a demand for sameness and an intolerance for change.

Dr. Shapiro is Professor of Psychiatry and Professor of Psychiatry in Pediatrics, Weill Medical College of Cornell University; Training and Supervising Analyst, The New York Psychoanalytic Institute.

Understanding Autism

Implications for Psychoanalysis

Fred Volkmar MD

Fred Volkmar

Child Study Center

Fred Volkmar  

Several lines of evidence inform current psychoanalytic thinking about infantile autism. Although early psychoanalytic interest in autism centered around the notion that experience might play a role in pathogenesis a large body of data suggest this is not the case; rather the condition appears to be the result of genetic and other neurobiological factors. Studies of children with autism do, however, suggest basic problems in capacities for object relations and other aspects of ego development which must be understood in the context of autistic social dysfunction. The study of normally developing infants raises considerable questions about the validity of notions such as a normal autistic phase; rather than for the normally developing child interest in the social world appears to be an innate capacity and one which has considerable importance for our understanding of the nature of early ego development and capacities for self-object differentiation.

A Response to the Contributors

Arnold Rothstein MD

Arnold Rothstein

275 Central Park West
New York, NY 10024

Arnold Rothstein  

In my “response to the contributors” I emphasize that I was moved to write my book in response to the question “Why are so many well-trained colleagues, young and old, having so much difficulty developing satisfying analytic practices?” To answer that question I proposed to explore my experience successfully developing and maintaining an analytic practice.

In attempting to answer the question I inadvertently stumbled upon a revolutionary (with a “small r”) answer to the problem. I discovered, in my attitudes and in my way of working in a consultation and the early phase of an analytic collaboration, a new “concrete puzzle solution” to the problem of how to help a prospective, often reluctant collaborator give analysis a “try.”

My book emphasizes my view that courses on “analyzability” and differential diagnosis are based on psychiatric rather than psychoanalytic diagnostic schema and may interfere with candidates' ability to learn how to create analytic patients.

Since I was a candidate, courses on analyzability have always seemed to me to resemble an exclusive club, deciding whom to exclude and whom to admit, rather than a procedure based on sound clinical experience. Analytic experience has demonstrated

Dr. Rothstein is Training and Supervising Analyst, the New York Psychoanalytic Institute.

611

that it is not possible in a consultation to predict accurately the outcome of an analysis. To make matters worse, it is probable that an analyst whose mind is focused on the task of evaluating a prospective analysand contributes to creating an environment in which certain patients are experienced as sicker than they might otherwise be.

In spite of the fact that it is not possible in a consultation to predict accurately the outcome of an analysis, many experienced “senior” analysts believe an analyst can and should be evaluative and selective. In their discussions of the subject, they focus primarily on characteristics of the patient rather than the match.

In my book I emphasize that in a consultation there are advantages in focusing on the patient's responses to the idea of engaging in a trial of analysis. The issue of the match and the particular time in their lives are significant from my perspective. The analyst's gender, age, personality, and related state of mind may be as important in effecting the outcome of a trial as any feature of the patient's mind.

My book shifts the emphasis of the focus of inquiry in a consultation from the patient to the analytic couple. It offers a different way of teaching candidates to work with prospective collaborators.

Henry Bachrach PHD

Henry Bachrach

Henry Bachrach  

Technical innovations always carry with them clinical and scientific challenges. The aim of this paper is to provide a context for exploring the consequences of technical innovations for psychoanalysis as an interrelated method of observation, treatment, and body of knowledge about mental functioning. The problems are approached from a methodological perspective because scientific progress requires methodological clarity. The inquiry begins with a methodological investigation of the technical and theoretical consequences of first principles, that is, the consequences of the assumptions and methods we adopt for the kind of data that are obtained by their application and for the theory required to understand and unify the resulting observations. The conclusion suggests that if one organizes a doctor-patient relationship around the clinical-historical and free-association methods with the aim of removing all obstacles to communication, if the understandings that emerge include a full range of dynamic, structural, genetic and adaptive propositions, one is engaged in psychoanalytic inquiry. Multiple Personality Disorder and One Analyst's Paradigm Shift

Richard Waugaman MD

Richard Waugaman

4701 Willard Avenue, #204
Chevy Chase, MD 20815

Richard Waugaman  

LAMENTABLY, RECENT DISCUSSIONS of multiple personality disorder (MPD) reflect sharp polarizations between those who accept the existence of this disorder as a genuine clinical entity (e.g., Putnam, 1989; Kluft, 1996) and those who believe it is either rare or iatrogenic, the joint creation of gullible therapists and suggestible patients (e.g., Merskey, 1992; Simpson, 1995). Until several years ago, I shared the opinion of the latter group. But more recently, my own clinical experience led me to change my mind (see also Waugaman, 1998, 1999, and Imperio, 1999). In this article, I will discuss this shift in my thinking about MPD. In my title, I borrow the concept of a paradigm shift with respect to MPD from the excellent article by Loewenstein and Ross (1992), who, in turn, borrowed the term from Thomas Kuhn (1970). I have found their discussion of the paradigm change involved in current theories of dissociative disorders to be a very useful way of understanding not only the evolution of my own thinking about MPD, but also then reaction of colleagues to these phenomena.

Dr. Waugaman is Training and Supervising Analyst, Washington Psychoanalytic Institute, and Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Georgetown University School of Medicine.

An earlier version of this paper was presented at the Chestnut Lodge Symposium, October 7, 1994.

Intimate Communications

The Values and Boundaries of Touch in the Psychoanalytic Setting

Ellen Ruderman PHD Psy.D.

Ellen Ruderman

16055 Ventura Boulevard, Suite 1110
Encino, CA 91436
eruderman@aol.com

Ellen Ruderman  

EACH PATIENT BRINGS TO ANALYSIS a unique lifetime of experience comprised of his or her own dynamics, archaic traumas, attachments, separations, and losses. The challenge for the analyst is how to approach these phenomena in the course of analytic treatment. One of the most highly charged questions that arises for many analysts is whether, with particular kinds of patients, nonerotic touch is appropriate and whether it has a place in the analytic milieu.

One of the most thought-provoking analyses of touch in psychoanalysis is Casement's paper (1982), “Some Pressures on the Analyst for Physical Contact During the Reliving of an Early Trauma.” The paper deals with the dilemma Casement faced with a patient's urgent expression of need for physical holding. He felt that actual touching would have been, for the patient, an avoidance rather than a working-through of a painful experience. If he had touched her, Casement felt he would have been rendered useless (what he called “a collapsed analyst”). Unable to bear the patient's psychic pain, he would have succumbed to her wish to have him leave his role. In fact, he believed he would have colluded with her in destroying a very consequential piece of the analysis.

Dr. Ruderman is Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst, Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Los Angeles, CA; Chair, Southern California Area Committee on Psychoanalysis in Clinical Social Work.

Seeking an Analytic Identity

Alan Skolnikoff MD

Alan Skolnikoff

205 Edgewood Avenue
San Francisco, CA 94117

Alan Skolnikoff  

Abstract

Rothstein has stimulated all analysts to rethink how we can better commit ourselves to our analytic work. In this paper I focus on factors in analysts' personalities and experiences in their training and practice that contribute to or distract from establishing an analytic identity.

First, I explore analysts' background and motivation. In admissions to psychoanalytic institutes we look for candidates who can see psychoanalysis as an intellectual puzzle to be solved and an emotional involvement to be experienced. We look for early conflicts that the candidate can sublimate in the service of analytic functioning. We assume that the capacity to sublimate is only partial and that analysts in their development continue to recognize conflicts in transference–countertransference reactions.

Second, I give some examples of experiences from analysts' training that stimulate the formation of their analytic identities. These include transient identifications and counter-identifications with the training analyst, supervisor, seminar leader, and favorite analytic authors.

Third, I discuss more external factors that influence the development of analytic identity. These include the climate in

Dr. Skolnikoff is Training and Supervising Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute; Associate Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, University of California, San Francisco.

594

training and continuing education at the institute. How much does the institute support its members in immersion in psychoanalysis? Economic factors continue to be an important factor in determining individual choice in this immersion.

Finally, I review studies on the effectiveness of psychoanalysis. Dedicated analysts with considerable experience believe that analysis works despite some limitations. Part of high motivation to continue analytic work includes understanding how analytic results differ from the simpler solutions achieved by nonanalytic therapies.

Prologue

On Disbelief

Richard Chefetz MD

Richard Chefetz

Richard Chefetz  

THIS ISSUE OF PSYCHOANALYTIC INQUIRY is about dissociative disorders and related subjects. It is this editor's effort to demystify area of inquiry that has had too long an association with disbelief. It was on my first day of residency training in psychiatry, a hot day at the beginning of July, that I was introduced to my first inpatients, two people with diagnoses of multiple personality disorder. I had thought this diagnosis to be quite rare. How did I get two patients, my first two, with the diagnosis? More provocative was the introduction to these people. I found their disorientation disorienting. I made appointments to see both of them in the next day or two. After I returned from the July 4th holiday, my service chief met me in the hall and invited me for an impromptu visit in her office. “Dr. Chefetz, do you really want to be here?” I was startled. Of course I wanted to be there! “Why did you make appointments with your new patients and then not keep them?” I was completely at a loss. I did not recall having made appointments, but I had a foggy sense that I had done so because that was on the agenda of my first inpatient day. I assured my chief that I very much wanted to be there and that I would promptly make new appointments and keep them. I was asked to stay “in touch.” I suppose that meant to contact her as well as to be in touch with reality. This was my introduction to fear in the countertransference and my own capacity to not know, to dissociate knowledge.

Recently, in a group supervision that I facilitate, an experienced clinician reported that their patient was being stalked and harassed by a group of sexual sadists, former friends of the patient, whom the patient had offended. With the report of the details of this case, other supervisees noted that they had become anxious, confused, and developed amnesia for portions of the clinical material presented.

Prologue

Susan Epstein CSW

Susan Epstein

Susan Epstein  

THE DISORDER KNOWN AS AUTISM HAS HAD A HISTORY fraught with controversy over its every aspect, including nomenclature, diagnosis and classification, etiology, and treatment. Despite considerable research and growing understanding, the disagreements and controversies over this still mysterious disorder remain. Contrary to conventional wisdom, autism is not a rare disorder. Recent epidemiological studies place the prevalence rate as high as one per 1000; if the full autism spectrum is included, this figure may be more than two per 1000. This would make disorders of the autism spectrum more common than Down syndrome or all combined forms of childhood cancer (Bristol et al., 1996; Rapin and Katzman, 1998).

One source of much confusion surrounding autism has to do with terminology. The word autism has been, and still is, used to refer both to the syndrome discussed here and to a psychological symptom or hypothesized primitive mental state (Bleuler, E. 1950; Mahler, 1952, 1955; Ogden, 1994; Tustin, 1993, 1995). Unfortunately, there is no term in widespread use that clearly differentiates the syndrome of autism from other uses of the word that are unrelated to it (Rutter, 1968). Despite an attempt by Kanner in his initial and subsequent writings to distinguish his use of the term early infantile autism from that used by Bleuler and other psychoanalytic writers, the autism of “Kanner's syndrome” rapidly became confused with these other concepts. Misapplication of concepts resulting from important early investigations into maternal deprivation, such as those in the works of A. Freud, Burlingham, and Spitz on institutionalized infants (A. Freud and Burlingham, 1944; Spitz, 1945, 1946) provided one such source of influence. The work of such authors as B. Rank (1949, 1955), Despert (1938, 1942, 1951), and most significantly Bettelheim (1959, 1967) incorporated these ideas and were major influences on the viewpoint of autism that predominated until sometime in the late 1960s to early 1970s.

Autism

A Brief History

Gary Mesibov PHD , Lynn Adams PHD and Eric Schopler PHD

Eric Schopler

Chapel Hill, NC 27599

Eric Schopler  

This paper discusses how the understanding of autism has changed in the 60 years since Leo Kanner first described the syndrome. Originally identified as an emotional disorder caused by parental ambivalence and rejection, autism today is universally seen as a neurobiological difficulty, whose cause is organic and related to atypical brain development. Evidence for the organic and genetic causes is presented, along with a discussion of how the understanding of autism has evolved during the past half century. The current understanding of autism as a developmental disorder has dramatically improved the quality of care and effectiveness of interventions for these youngsters and their families.

Herbert Schlesinger PHD and Ann Appelbaum MD

Ann Appelbaum

45 East 85th Street

Ann Appelbaum  

Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father.1

And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all.2

TOUCHING, THE “LAYING ON OF HANDS,” has had a central place in all systems of healing practice since time immemorial, but attitudes about it increasingly became mixed as medicine became more “scientific.” In the past, doctors applied their ears to the chest of the patient to hear the breath sounds and heartbeat and to the abdomen to hear the sounds of the bowel. The stethoscope, EKG, and X-ray, and later the CAT scan, MRI, and sonography, placed increasing distance between the patient's skin and the doctor's ears, eyes, and hands, so that direct examination of the patient has become increasingly perfunctory. The fear and awe of the body and of the laying on of hands that every medical student must overcome is suppressed by objectifying the body.

Dr. Schlesinger is Alfred J. and Monette C. Marrow Professor of Psychology, Emeritus, New School for Social Research; Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Centre for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.

Dr. Appelbaum is Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons; Instructor, Columbia University Centre for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.
